source.title: Rethinking Activation Functions: Reducing Bias Can Improve Learning
source.authors: Zi-Rui Peng; Helen Zheng; Zi-Ming Liu

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent truncation.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares training outcomes under an activation-bias intervention, but it does not test the claim versions’ specific error, depth, initialization, learning-rate, or normalization outcomes.
record.gate_note: The study reports training-loss and performance comparisons after shifting activations. These do not measure near-zero training classification error, the named depth/shortcut effect, initialization effects, learning-rate stability, or batch-normalization speed. Rows are recorded as findings about training outcomes that fit none of the listed versions. Figure-only comparisons are represented only where the text describes their direction; no values are inferred from plots.
record.test_reason: The study tests activation shifting, rather than any listed claim version. Its loss, curvature, and hidden-state results do not establish training classification error, spurious-minimum frequency, depth degradation prevented by shortcuts, initialization-dependent trainability, stability-threshold dynamics, or batch-normalization benefits. References to those topics provide context.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. In controlled models, reducing activation bias slows early learning while producing smoother trajectories, lower curvature, and lower final loss. Across the larger settings studied, shifting improves late-stage performance, although ViT retains higher training loss and GPT-2 lacks the initial unshifted advantage. The authors do not claim universal benefit or a complete causal explanation.
record.recipe_differences: The paper varies fixed or adaptive activation shifts to study activation bias; it does not use the claim’s named training-error, shortcut, initialization, learning-rate, or normalization comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that early acceleration, overshoot, and final-performance differences may depend on data and task, model scale, architecture, and initialization. In GPT-2 Small, the unshifted model did not show the initial advantage seen in the controlled model.

fits_no_version.finding: Controlled residual teacher–student models learn more slowly initially after activation shifting but ultimately reach lower loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reducing activation bias can trade slower initial learning for lower final loss in controlled residual teacher–student models.

fits_no_version.finding: Adaptive shifting increases ViT training loss, yields comparable or lower DiT training loss, and reduces GPT-2 language-model loss by approximately 0.01.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation shifting affects optimization differently across architectures and tasks; improved final performance need not entail lower training loss.

fits_no_version.finding: The shifted VGG-style autoencoder has higher reconstruction loss initially and lower loss later.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reducing activation bias can reverse the relative reconstruction-loss ordering over training.

record.problems: Several comparisons are described from figures without numeric values or uncertainty estimates. The authors state that the larger-model experiments do not systematically test whether all controlled-setting phenomena generalize, and that they lack a unified mathematical theory or complete causal account.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for test loss, accuracy, FID, perplexity, or activation-component reconstruction: those measures do not bear on the listed versions’ named outcomes. Additional scale-up results in Appendix E are described as performance results but do not report the relevant training classification error or other version-specific measures. Figure-only hidden-state trajectories and loss-landscape measurements concern dynamics rather than the listed version outcomes.

untested.parts: Near-zero CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 training classification error, random or corrupted labels, and size, stopping, or regularization effects.
Spurious local minima in two-layer ReLU teacher–student models and their reduction through one or two extra student neurons.
Depth-dependent training-error degradation in plain networks, prevention through identity shortcuts, and the named alternative training recipes.
Initialization comparisons establishing faster learning, stable signal or gradient propagation, or increased trainable depth. Estimating an activation shift at initialization does not test these.

Recovery or divergence around learning-rate stability limits and sharpness approaching or tracking the stability threshold. Lower curvature under activation shifting does not establish these dynamics.

Batch normalization versus no normalization for training speed or learning-rate tolerance, and normalization-free Fixup comparisons. Adaptive neuronwise centering is not a batch-normalization comparison.

record.verdict_notes: Correct the record's tests/T2 classification to discusses/T6. All five rows describe original findings, but none measures a listed version. The appendix's width/depth sweeps compare activation-shift benefits, not spurious-minimum rates or plain-versus-residual degradation. No version-relevant missing results were identified.

versions.untested_parts: Does not report training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, or the stated size, early-stopping, and regularization comparisons.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student sweep over teacher and student neuron counts or spurious-minimum outcomes.
Does not compare plain and shortcut networks across depth for training classification error, or test the stated special-initialization and normalization-free recipes.
Does not compare the listed initializations or measure trainable depth under them.
Does not sweep learning rates around a stability threshold or report the stated curvature and divergence behavior.
Does not compare batch normalization with no normalization for training speed or learning-rate tolerance, or test Fixup.

rows.subject: Controlled teacher–student model (both students; aggregate across ReLU, GELU, Swish, and Sigmoid)
rows.operation_detail: Compared unshifted activations with a fixed post-activation shift while holding teacher, initialization, data, and optimization settings constant.
rows.value: shifted student learns more slowly initially, then overtakes and reaches lower final loss
rows.note: The comparison concerns loss, not classification error; the text gives no numeric loss values.
rows.check: The reported early-to-late loss reversal is supported, but this is a deep residual, LayerNorm teacher–student model, not V2's two-layer ReLU width experiment. Common initialization is controlled rather than varied.

rows.subject: ViT-Base
rows.operation_detail: Compared adaptive activation shifting with the unshifted baseline under otherwise fixed training choices.
rows.value: adaptive-shift model retains a higher training loss
rows.note: The paper states the direction of the training-loss comparison, not classification training error or its magnitude.
rows.check: Higher training loss under adaptive shifting is correctly reported. The original partial state has no applicable claim version: neither near-zero classification error nor a listed intervention is measured.

rows.subject: DiT-B/2
rows.operation_detail: Compared adaptive activation shifting with the unshifted baseline under otherwise fixed training choices.
rows.value: adaptive shifting achieves comparable or lower training loss throughout training
rows.note: This is an image-generation loss comparison, not classification error.
rows.check: Comparable or lower diffusion training loss is correctly reported, but cannot establish any listed version. Replace the original observed state.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Small
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch for 300,000 optimization steps
rows.operation_detail: Compared adaptive activation shifting with the unshifted baseline under otherwise fixed training choices.
rows.value: adaptive shifting stably lowers loss by about 0.01 in absolute terms
rows.note: The paper also reports perplexity 1% lower relative to the unshifted baseline; that is a separate metric but does not bear on a listed version.
rows.check: The approximately 0.01 loss reduction is supported, but bears on no listed version. Section 4.3 does not explicitly identify this loss as training versus evaluation loss; retain the generic language-model-loss description.

rows.subject: Simplified VGG-style autoencoder (both models; aggregate comparison)
rows.size_stated: VGG-19 encoder with 512 channels at each latent spatial location
rows.operation_detail: Compared otherwise identical models using unshifted and shifted activations.
rows.value: shifted model initially has higher loss but achieves lower loss later
rows.note: The text provides no numeric losses; this is reconstruction rather than classification.
rows.check: The reconstruction-loss reversal is supported but bears on no listed version. Describe the encoder as using part of VGG-19, rather than implying the complete VGG-19 encoder.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
